passage:
I'm Samir, and I sit two desks from Sudha. Last Thursday her report was praised in the team meeting. "Oh, it's nothing," she said, waving a hand. "Honestly, I'm hopeless with these things, anyone could have done it." Then she looked around the table and waited. Two colleagues jumped in with "No, no, it was great." She smiled and said, "You're too kind."
She says some version of this most weeks. Afterwards she checks her phone, and I've seen her reread the group thread for replies. I can't know what she feels. Maybe she really doubts herself. But I've started to feel awkward, not sure whether to praise her again or stay quiet, and today I stayed quiet.

qa.q: What did Sudha say when her report was praised?
qa.a: She said it was nothing and that she was hopeless with these things and anyone could have done it.

qa.q: What is Samir feeling while watching Sudha's pattern repeat?
qa.a: Samir feels awkward and unsure whether to give more praise or stay quiet. That is why Samir stayed silent today.

qa.q: What could Samir try instead of adding to the praise or staying silent?
qa.a: Samir could name one specific thing liked in the report and then ask what Sudha found hard about it. That gives a real conversation without feeding a routine.

qa.q: What might Sudha want when she says she is hopeless and then looks around the table?
qa.a: She may want reassurance or recognition. Waiting and rereading the thread suggest she hopes for more praise, though Samir cannot be sure of her inner state.

grounding: A colleague notices someone say she is nothing while seeming to wait for praise.

passage:
Tuesday, the client approved Sachin's layout. In the corridor he sighed to Rafiq. "I'm nothing, really. Just lucky. You do the real work here." He looked up, waiting. Rafiq said, "Come on, that's not true, it looked great," and Sachin gave a modest little laugh.
Thursday, at lunch, Sachin mentioned the same thing. "Honestly, I'm the weakest designer on the floor." Rafiq noticed he had said it right after a colleague walked past. He noticed, too, that Sachin's eyes went to his face each time, checking.
The following Monday it happened again. This time Rafiq said, "The colour choice was yours and it worked. Is there something in it you're unsure about?" Sachin blinked. After a pause he said quietly, "Actually, the spacing bothers me." They pulled up the file and looked at it together.

qa.q: What did Sachin say to Rafiq in the corridor on Tuesday?
qa.a: He said he was nothing, just lucky, and that Rafiq did the real work.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling by the third time Sachin said he was nothing?
qa.a: Rafiq was uneasy and a little wary, having noticed Sachin said it soon after someone walked past and glanced at Rafiq's face each time. Still, Rafiq cared enough to answer differently.

qa.q: What changed when Rafiq answered differently on Monday?
qa.a: Rafiq named something specific and asked an open question. Sachin then admitted a real worry about the spacing, and they worked on it together.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt when Rafiq's question skipped the usual reassurance?
qa.a: Probably surprised, since he blinked and paused. He may have felt caught out, and also relieved to say something true.

grounding: A colleague notices someone repeatedly say he is nothing while looking for praise, and the pattern shows over three days.

passage: "Sit, Vasudha, the tea will go cold," said Harish uncle, pushing a plate of biscuits across. "You asked how to handle that teammate who keeps saying she's useless. Let me tell you about Prakash. When I was new at the insurance office, Prakash would finish a report and sigh, 'Arre, I'm nothing, just a small clerk, this is probably full of mistakes.' Then he'd stand there. Waiting. The first month, I rushed to tell him it was brilliant. By the third month I noticed he only said it when the manager was near, and only about his best work. I felt a bit foolish for falling for it, and a bit sorry for him. One day I just said, 'Looks solid, Prakash,' and went back to my desk. He looked lost. Later he started asking me to check his numbers for real, and those were our best conversations."

qa.q: What did Prakash say after finishing a report?
qa.a: He would sigh, 'Arre, I'm nothing, just a small clerk, this is probably full of mistakes,' and then stand there waiting.

qa.q: How did Harish feel once he noticed the pattern?
qa.a: Harish felt a bit foolish for having rushed to praise Prakash, and also a bit sorry for him.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Harish and Prakash related?
qa.a: The day Harish answered with a plain 'Looks solid, Prakash' instead of gushing; after that Prakash began asking for real checks of his numbers.

qa.q: What might Prakash have been hoping for each time he called himself nothing?
qa.a: He seemed to want praise and notice, especially near the manager, but without asking for it openly.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing that someone's repeated self-putdowns were really a quiet request for praise.

passage: The quarterly review had fifteen minutes before the conference room was handed to another team, and the projector kept flickering. Tushar presented the new onboarding flow, then clicked to the last slide and spread his hands. "Honestly, I'm nobody here. I just stayed up three nights and redid everything, but it's really the team's work." He looked slowly around the table. Manjula had seen this before. At the offsite he'd said, "I'm no speaker," right before a twenty-minute talk. She glanced at Deepa, who was already studying her notebook. Someone murmured, "Great job, Tushar," flatly. The manager nodded and said, "Next item, we're short on time." Tushar sat down, jaw tight. Manjula caught him later by the water cooler. "The flow is good," she said. "You don't have to shrink it to show it."

qa.q: How many nights did Tushar say he stayed up?
qa.a: He said he stayed up three nights and redid everything.

qa.q: What was Manjula thinking as Tushar looked around the table?
qa.a: Manjula seemed wary and a little tired of it, because she had seen him do the same at the offsite and recognised the pattern of fishing for praise.

qa.q: What made Manjula's words at the water cooler a kind response?
qa.a: She gave Tushar honest, specific credit for the flow while gently naming that he did not need the false modesty, in private rather than in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt when the room responded flatly?
qa.a: Tushar was probably hurt and frustrated, since the praise he was angling for came out weak and the meeting moved on.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a teammate's 'I'm nobody' line as a bid for praise that others also saw through.

passage: Kiran leaned back from the monitor at the wedding-design studio in Kalkaji. On the screen was an invitation of peacock blues and gold, so good that the intern gasped. "Oh, this? I'm not a real designer, I just threw it together in an hour," Kiran said, then waited, eyes moving from face to face. Kashish, at the next desk, had heard "I'm not a real designer" four times this month, always about the best pieces, always loud enough for the owner to hear. The intern said, "It's stunning!" Kiran smiled and said, "No, no, it's rubbish." Kashish noticed the owner's small eye-roll before turning back to a client call. At lunch the intern whispered, "Does Kiran always do that?" Kashish shrugged. "It's beautiful work. I wish Kiran would just say so."

qa.q: How long did Kiran say the invitation took?
qa.a: Kiran said it was thrown together in an hour.

qa.q: What does Kashish seem to feel about Kiran's remarks, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Kashish had counted the line four times this month and noticed it always came with the best work and within the owner's hearing, which suggests mild irritation rather than admiration.

qa.q: What could Kiran try instead when showing strong work?
qa.a: Kiran could say something simple like 'I'm really happy with this one' and let people react honestly, without the put-down.

qa.q: How does the intern see Kiran's 'it's rubbish' reply?
qa.a: The intern is at first taken in and impressed, but by lunch is puzzled enough to ask whether Kiran always does it.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a humble-brag and that others in the studio also saw through it.

passage:
In the office pantry, Sabina sighed over her coffee. "Honestly, I'm so bad at presentations. The client only asked for my deck in the follow-up because they felt sorry for me."
"No way," said Nikhil. "It was brilliant!"
"Stop, it was nothing. Just three all-nighters." Sabina glanced sideways. "Right, Sharmila? Nothing special?"
Sharmila stirred her tea. "The data slide was really strong. The ending ran a bit long."
Sabina's smile flickered. "Oh. Yeah. Totally." She picked up her mug and left.
Nikhil leaned in. "Did she want us to argue with her?"
"I think she wanted us to say it was amazing," Sharmila said quietly, "without having to say it herself."
"Why not just say she's proud of it?"
Sharmila rinsed her cup. "Maybe fishing feels safer than asking."

qa.q: What did Sabina say the client asked for in the follow-up?
qa.a: She said the client asked for her deck in the follow-up.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when she gave Sabina balanced feedback instead of praise?
qa.a: She seemed a little uncomfortable with the fishing for compliments and chose to be kind but honest, naming the strong data slide and the long ending.

qa.q: What could Sabina say the next time she is proud of her work?
qa.a: She could say, "I worked hard on this and I'm pleased with it. Any feedback?", which invites real praise and real notes without pretending.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt when Sharmila's reply was balanced?
qa.a: She probably felt deflated and a bit exposed, since her smile flickered when the praise she was fishing for did not come.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing someone call their own work nothing while fishing for praise, and others quietly seeing through it.
